deep.reconstruction:
Orientation: the page is written upside down relative to the scan. The machine transcription of the main formulas is badly garbled. Almost every 'dx/dx', 'dx/ds', 'dx/x' is really α/x, α/2 or x/α. Context from the previous page: Riemann is studying a degenerate (confluent) hypergeometric equation, x v'' + (−2εx + 1/2) v' + ((ε²−1)x + α − ε/2) v = 0. It arises as the limit n→∞ of factors like (1 − x/n)^{n/2}(1 + x/n)^{n/2+α/2}, giving e^{±x}. He builds series solutions with Γ-factors Π(μ − 3/4 + α/(2ε)). This page attacks the large-parameter behaviour of a Laplace-type integral representation of such solutions,
  ∫ e^{−xs} (1+s)^{α/2+…} (1−s)^{−α/2+…} ds,
by the method of steepest descent.

(1) Phase function. Riemann sets
  y(s) = −x s + (α/2) log((1+s)/(1−s)).
The integrand is then e^{y}, up to slowly varying factors.

(2) Saddle points. He writes
  dy/ds = −x + (α/2)(1/(1+s) + 1/(1−s)) = −x + α/(1−s²) = 0,
equivalently 1 + (x/α)(s² − 1) = 0, or s² − 1 + α/x = 0. Hence
  s = ±√(1 − α/x).

(3) Two regimes. In the figure the two regimes are labelled x > α and x < α.
- For x > α the two saddles are real and lie between −1 and +1.
- For x < α they are purely imaginary.
- At x = α they coalesce at s = 0.
A garbled line, apparently −α/x … = 2x/α …(1+…)², seems to concern the second derivative, y''(s) = 2αs/(1−s²)². This is my reading.

(4) Substitution. He sets t = (1+s)/(1−s), so s = (t−1)/(t+1), turning the logarithm into log t. That is, the integrand becomes e^{−xs} t^{α/2}.

(5) Value at the saddle (my reading). Lines containing (1−s²)/s and log((1+s)/(1−s)) evaluate y at the saddle. With x = α/(1−s₀²),
  y(s₀) = α[ −s₀/(1−s₀²) + ½ log((1+s₀)/(1−s₀)) ],
and the next line differentiates this.

(6) Figure. Small circles surround the branch points s = ±1, labelled +1, −1 with ±∞ (the values of the logarithm). Large loop contours come in from infinity. In the upper sketch they pass through the saddles on the real segment between the circles (x > α). In the lower sketch they pass through conjugate points above and below the real axis (x < α). The curves fanning out of the saddles are clearly steepest-descent and level lines.

(7) Lower part, uncertain. The lower lines contain:
- x(1/3 − u + λ(1 − 3u)),
- a factor (3u² − 1/u),
- ∂²x/∂u² u² + ∂x/∂u (3u² − …) + …,
- a change of variable ∂v/∂u = x… .
They look like an attempt to derive a second-order ODE in a new variable u near the coalescence point. The cubic coefficient 1/3 is consistent with y ≈ (α−x)s + α s³/3 near s = 0. Too garbled to reconstruct with certainty.
errors: No mathematical error is detectable in the legible part: dy/ds and the saddle condition s² = 1 − α/x are correct.
The lower ODE manipulations are too fragmentary to check; several struck-out attempts show trial and error.
The machine transcription systematically misreads α as 'dx' (e.g. α/2 → dx/ds, α/x → dx/x).

results.what: Saddle points of the phase −xs + (α/2)log((1+s)/(1−s)) at s = ±√(1−α/x), with real vs. imaginary saddles for x > α vs. x < α and coalescence at x = α
results.modern_name: Method of steepest descent / saddle-point method for confluent hypergeometric (Whittaker/Laguerre-type) integrals; coalescing saddles (turning point)
results.usually_credited_to: Riemann (1863 fragment on hypergeometric series, publ. 1876), Debye (1909); uniform treatment of coalescing saddles: Chester–Friedman–Ursell (1957)

results.what: Sketch of steepest-descent contours around branch points ±1 through the saddles in both regimes
Possible reduction near coalescence to a cubic phase (Airy-type) via an ODE in a new variable u
results.usually_credited_to: Stokes (1850s, Airy integral), later Langer, Chester–Friedman–Ursell

deep.surprise_reason: Riemann's use of the saddle-point method is already known (1863 hypergeometric fragment; Riemann–Siegel formula). This page shows it applied to a confluent hypergeometric integral with an explicit picture of two regimes and coalescing saddles at x = α. If the bundle's 1853 dating is right, it predates his other known uses. That is a notable unpublished detail but not a new attribution, and the transition analysis is only fragmentary.
